title: SYSK Selects: Gesundheit! How Allergies Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of an episode on allergies. Josh and Chuck explain allergies as an immune system case of mistaken identity: lymphocytes (T and B cells), antigens, sensitizing exposure, IgE antibodies binding to mast cells and basophils that carry histamine, and the allergic cascade producing symptoms. They cover severe reactions (anaphylaxis and anaphylactic shock), epinephrine (EpiPen) and its limited 10 to 20 minute duration, allergy testing (scratch test and blood tests), management (avoidance, medication, immunotherapy), Chuck's personal shrimp allergy and immunotherapy experience, and a listener mail about a stuntman's fire scene in the film In the Name of the Father. Includes a sponsor break.

entities.name: In the Name of the Father

segments.title: Opening banter and allergy season
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode, explaining he picked it because of a rough pollen season. The hosts chat about Chuck's cold-like symptoms, Emily's allergies, and a TV-show bee sting story.

segments.title: Allergies as mistaken identity
segments.summary: Allergy is defined as an immune overreaction to a perceived invader, a case of mistaken identity often linked to proteins such as shrimp protein or bee venom.

segments.title: Lymphocytes, T cells and B cells
segments.summary: The hosts describe lymphocytes such as T cells and B cells as white blood cells that patrol the body and investigate cells; B cells in the lymph nodes turn into plasma cells that produce antibodies against an antigen.

segments.title: IgE antibodies, mast cells and histamine
segments.summary: Five antibody types are named, with IgE responsible for allergic reactions. IgE binds to mast cells and basophils, which contain histamine, and the first contact is the sensitizing exposure.

segments.title: The allergic cascade and symptoms
segments.summary: Complement proteins lock on and cause mast cells or basophils to rupture, releasing histamine. It can take seven to ten days after sensitization for the cascade to occur. Symptoms include sneezing, hives, nausea and swelling.

segments.title: Anaphylaxis, anaphylactic shock and EpiPen
segments.summary: Severe reactions can progress to anaphylaxis and anaphylactic shock, which can be fatal within minutes. Epinephrine (EpiPen) opens airways, but its effect lasts only about ten to twenty minutes, and several hundred US deaths a year are mentioned.

segments.title: Peanut allergies and airline policy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the difficulty of avoiding peanuts and a flight where peanuts were banned due to a passenger's allergy.

segments.title: Allergy testing and treatment options
segments.summary: Testing includes scratch tests and blood tests for specific antigens. Treatment options are avoidance, medication such as corticosteroids and antihistamines, and immunotherapy.

segments.title: Immunotherapy and personal experiences
segments.summary: Immunotherapy is described as gradual allergy shots that may build blocking IgG antibodies, and still somewhat controversial. Emily has been on allergy shots, and Chuck describes overcoming a shrimp allergy by gradually eating shrimp chips.

segments.title: Listener mail: stuntman on fire
segments.summary: A listener named Freddie Turner from Oxford, England, shares a story of his father, an actor who was set on fire for a prison scene in In the Name of the Father and had to wait for the director to say action.
